It is graded uncertain rather than present because the town's population roughly quadrupled between the roster and the scene date and a great many of the men on it were, in Andreas's own phrase, 'adventurers, comprising moneyed speculators and prospectors, as yet undecided whether to stay at Chicago or go on'.

persons.name: Alanson Sweet

occupation.note: 'Alanson Sweet, 1832' in the roster, with no trade. Andreas supplies it elsewhere: 'In 1833, the first Tremont House, situated then on the northwest corner of Lake and Dearborn streets, was built by Alanson Sweet. It was kept as a saloon and boarding-house by him and a man from Canada, named Darwin.'

persons.note: Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 (scan p. 281), 'an imperfect list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, not before named'. It gives a name, a trade and usually an arrival year, and it is a retrospective of 1884: a YEAR off it is documented, a MONTH is not, and it says nothing whatever about 1835. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Sweet, Alanson” (tax_1833_099, line 151); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Sweet, Alanson” (poll_1834_105, line 274); Poll list of 1835 — “Sweet, Alanson” (poll_1835_078, line 365). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Sweet' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

resident_research.evidence_for: forenames agree initial for initial: entry 'Alanson Sweet' against resident 'Alanson Sweet'

research_note: THE MAN WHO BUILT THE TREMONT AND SOLD IT. He put the house up in 1833, kept it as a saloon and boarding house with a Canadian named Darwin, and the Couch brothers then bought it - which is why Ira Couch and not Alanson Sweet is linked to tremont_house_1 in this parcel. What Sweet was doing on 1 July 1835 is not stated anywhere reached, and the occupation recorded here is the one he is documented in rather than the one he then had. HIS PARTNER DARWIN IS A DOCUMENTED RESIDENT WITH A SURNAME, A TRADE AND AN ORIGIN ('a man from Canada') and is not written as a household, because a boarding-house partner in 1833 whose given name is unknown and who is never mentioned again is exactly the kind of entry that would inflate the count without adding evidence. He is recorded in data/residents/index.json among the people researched and not written.
